system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted after an unwitnessed fall while intoxicated, presenting with chest pain. Imaging revealed six left-sided rib fractures and a small, stable left apical pneumothorax that resolved without intervention. He experienced transient confusion that resolved with supportive care. On hospital day two, he developed abdominal distension and vomiting; a KUB showed gastric distention, prompting NG tube placement, which was removed the following day after improvement. His pain was managed with a transition from PCA morphine to oral oxycodone. His multiple myeloma was stable, though his platelet count was low, leading to temporary discontinuation of warfarin. He was discharged to a sub-acute rehabilitation facility with instructions for pain management, incentive spirometry, and follow-up with his oncology team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You’re here because you’ve been having shortness of breath and fevers since leaving rehab. Can you tell me more about how you’ve been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been really short of breath, especially when I try to take a deep breath. It hurts on my left side. And I’ve had fevers—up to 102.3 at rehab. I also felt dizzy and my blood pressure was high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned they might have given you too much insulin at rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they gave me 60 units of Lantus instead of 30. That’s why my sugars were in the 40s. I told them, but I’m not sure they listened.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could definitely cause low sugars. We’ll adjust your insulin here. We’ve done a chest X-ray, and it shows a moderate fluid collection on your left side—bigger than before. Given your recent rib fractures, we’re concerned it might be blood collecting there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Blood? From the ribs? But I thought that was healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes the injury can cause delayed bleeding. We’re doing a CT scan to check for that and to rule out a blood clot in your lungs. We also saw a new area of consolidation in your right lung—could be pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pneumonia? I haven’t had a cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You might not always cough. When you’re in pain from rib fractures, you tend to ‘splint’—breathe shallowly—which can lead to lung infections. We’ll start antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. Good news—no blood clot in your lungs and no active bleeding. But the fluid on your left side has grown and isn’t hemorrhagic. We’re worried it’s compressing your lung.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what do we do about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We may need to drain it. We’ll also start IV antibiotics for the pneumonia. Your white blood cell count is low, which is common with your myeloma, so we want to be aggressive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I feel dizzy again. My head’s been pounding since this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure was high earlier—190s. We gave medication, and it’s down to 140s, but you’re still feeling off?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, and my left hand feels clumsy. I missed my mouth when I tried to drink water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I noticed some nystagmus—eye twitching—when you looked to the left. And you’re a bit unsteady. We’ll get a brain MRI to rule out a stroke, but given your history of neuropathy, this might be related to that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI is clear—no stroke or new brain issue. Neurology thinks your dizziness and coordination issues are due to neuropathy from diabetes and myeloma. We’ll manage it with slow position changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no stroke? That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No stroke. But we do need to address the fluid in your chest. We’re going to place a chest tube to drain it. It’s a quick procedure, and it should help you breathe better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve just placed a chest tube. We drained about 1200 cc of serosanguinous fluid—old blood mixed with fluid. Your lung should start re-expanding now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a lot of fluid. Does that explain why I’ve been so short of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The fluid was pressing on your lung. We’ll monitor the drainage, and once it slows, we’ll remove the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound of your belly to check for internal bleeding, since your hemoglobin dropped. No bleeding there. Your liver shows fatty changes, likely from past alcohol use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had a history with that. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s consistent with steatosis. We’ll monitor it, but the priority now is your chest and infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your hemoglobin has dropped to 6.7. Given the fluid we drained and your low counts, we’re going to give you one unit of blood to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of the blood in the fluid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely, yes. The pleural fluid had a low red cell count, so it’s probably an old hemothorax. Your anemia is also related to your myeloma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The fluid we drained was tested. No infection or cancer cells. It’s an exudate, likely from the trauma. We’re confident it won’t come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on IV antibiotics—vancomycin and cefepime—for five days. You’re no longer febrile, so we’re switching to oral levofloxacin for ten days total. You’ll finish the course at rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain? Are you able to move better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It still hurts, but the pain meds help. I’m getting up a bit more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep using the incentive spirometer. It helps prevent another pneumonia. We’ve increased your oxycodone to manage pain with activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows the lung is re-expanding. The chest tube drainage has slowed. We’ll likely remove it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’m ready to get this out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve removed the chest tube. Another X-ray confirms your lung is staying open. No air leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can already breathe a little deeper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll keep you on antibiotics and pain meds. Your myeloma team wants you to follow up within a week. Your platelets are stable, but your oncologist will decide when to restart treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood thinners? I was on warfarin for clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held it because of your low platelets and rib fractures. Your provider will reassess whether you need to restart it after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your infection markers are improving. Hemoglobin is stable after the transfusion. We’re on track for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Back to rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to the same facility. We’ll send detailed instructions on your meds, wound care, and activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re confirming your discharge meds. We’ve lowered your Lantus to 25 units at night to prevent low morning sugars. You’ll continue the sliding scale for highs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take 5 mg every four hours as needed. Take it before therapy or walking to stay ahead of the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue moving slowly when getting up. Your neuropathy won’t change quickly, but being cautious will help prevent falls.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final chest X-ray shows stable findings. The left side is still a bit cloudy, but that’s expected. You’re cleared for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad to be going back. I just want to keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Keep up the breathing exercises, take your antibiotics fully, and follow up with your oncologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing your discharge. You’re breathing better, off oxygen, and walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pneumonia is resolving, the fluid is gone, and your pain is controlled. You’ll continue levofloxacin for five more days. Finish all of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll take the pain meds before therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Also, keep using the incentive spirometer. And remember—stand up slowly. Your dizziness is from nerve damage, not your heart or brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Your rehab team has your plan. Call us if you develop fever, chest pain, or shortness of breath. Otherwise, see you at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check—your discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to leave whenever the transport is scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. Stay on top of your health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is here. Nurse will wheel you out. Have a safe trip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you understand all your medications and when to follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve gone over them with the nurse. I have my prescriptions and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Call if anything changes. You’ve made great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your blood test showed anemia related to your myeloma and the blood loss into the chest. We transfused one unit, and you’re stable. Your oncologist will monitor this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll bring it up at my appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And keep taking the thiamine and B complex—we added those for your history of alcohol use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I know it’s important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The team here has done a great job, and so have you. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’m ready to get back to rehab and keep moving forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the spirit. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check-in before you go. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Thanks for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you soon for follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was readmitted with shortness of breath, fevers, and dizziness eleven days after discharge to rehab following a fall with rib fractures. Imaging revealed a moderate left pleural effusion, concerning for hemothorax, and a new right lower lobe consolidation suggestive of pneumonia. He was treated for healthcare-associated pneumonia with intravenous vancomycin and cefepime, later transitioned to oral levofloxacin. A chest tube was placed, draining 1200 cc of serosanguinous fluid, with resolution of the effusion and improvement in respiratory status. He developed dizziness and left-sided coordination issues, but MRI brain showed no acute abnormality; neurology attributed symptoms to neuropathy. His hemoglobin dropped to 6.7 g/dL, prompting a single unit of packed red blood cells. His diabetes was managed with adjustment of Lantus dose to prevent hypoglycemia. He was discharged to the same rehab facility on oral antibiotics, pain control, and instructions for slow mobilization due to neuropathy and fall risk.
